descriptor: The largest wild dog, living and hunting in family packs across the forests, tundra and steppe of the north.

physical.fact: Its jaws hold 42 teeth, and it can sprint at up to about 56 km/h.

range.summary: Across much of North America, Europe and Asia, from Arctic tundra to deserts. Wolves are recolonising western Europe and parts of the United States after near extermination.
regions: Siberia and the Russian Far East

source.label: Wisconsin DNR, Annual Wolf Report 2026 and Gray Wolf Monitoring Report 2020

population.note: Counts from 1980 to 2020 are minimum late-winter counts from snow tracking and radio collars. The 2026 figure is a model-based estimate with a 95% credible interval, so it is not strictly comparable.

threats.title: Conflict over livestock
threats.detail: Attacks on sheep and cattle lead to legal culls and illegal retaliatory killing.

threats.title: Hunting and poaching
threats.detail: Wolves are hunted or trapped across much of their range, legally and illegally.

threats.title: Roads and fragmentation
threats.detail: Vehicle collisions are a leading cause of death for dispersing wolves in Europe.

threats.title: Hybridisation with dogs
threats.detail: Free-roaming dogs interbreed with wolves in parts of southern Europe and Asia.

places.name: Lamar Valley, Yellowstone National Park
places.note: Open valley where reintroduced packs are watched daily through spotting scopes.

places.name: Denali National Park
places.note: Wolves are sometimes seen from the park road in summer.

places.name: Algonquin Provincial Park
places.note: Famous public wolf howls on August evenings.

places.name: Sierra de la Culebra
places.note: Stronghold of the Iberian wolf with guided dawn watches.

places.name: Abruzzo, Lazio and Molise National Park
places.note: Apennine wolves that survived when the species vanished from most of western Europe.

sightings.tip: Winter is best in Yellowstone, when snow makes wolves easy to spot against open slopes and elk herds move to lower valleys. Algonquin's howls run in August.

actions.title: Support non-lethal livestock protection
actions.detail: Guardian dogs, electric fencing and night pens cut losses without killing wolves.

actions.title: Keep dogs vaccinated and under control
actions.detail: Loose dogs spread disease to wolves and can hybridise with them.

actions.title: Watch wolves ethically
actions.detail: Keep your distance, never feed wildlife and stay on roads and trails.

actions.title: Back wildlife crossings
actions.detail: Overpasses and underpasses on busy roads reduce collisions and reconnect populations.

regions.name: Northern Minnesota
regions.note: Minnesota kept the last large wolf population in the lower 48 states and seeded the Great Lakes return.

regions.name: Northern Wisconsin
regions.note: Wiped out by 1960, wolves crossed back into Wisconsin from Minnesota in the mid-1970s.

regions.name: Upper Peninsula, Michigan
regions.note: A pair in Michigan's Upper Peninsula produced the first verified pups there in 1991.

regions.name: Yellowstone
regions.note: 14 wolves from Alberta were released in Yellowstone in 1995; its last pack was killed in 1926.

regions.name: Blue Range, Arizona
regions.note: The first 11 captive-bred Mexican wolves were released in the Blue Range in 1998.

regions.name: Colorado
regions.note: Colorado released its first reintroduced wolves in Grand County in December 2023.

regions.name: Chihuahua and Durango
regions.note: By 1980 the last few wild Mexican wolves in Chihuahua and Durango had been caught for breeding.

regions.name: Italian Apennines
regions.note: About 100 wolves survived in the Apennines in the 1970s and later spread north into the Alps.

regions.name: Mercantour, France
regions.note: Two wolves from Italy were seen in France's Mercantour National Park in 1992.

regions.name: Lusatia, Germany
regions.note: In 2000 wolves from Poland raised Germany's first wild pups in about 150 years.

regions.name: Jutland, Denmark
regions.note: A wolf found in Thy in 2012 was Denmark's first since 1813; a pack settled in Jutland in 2017.

regions.name: Varmland, Sweden
regions.note: Functionally extinct in Scandinavia by the 1960s, wolves bred again in Varmland in 1983.

rangeHistory.note: A selection of documented losses and returns; wolves also came back to Idaho, the Netherlands, Belgium and more.

summary.text: The wolf, also known as the grey wolf or gray wolf, is a canine native to Eurasia and North America. More than thirty subspecies of Canis lupus have been recognized, including the dog and dingo, though grey wolves, as popularly understood, include only naturally occurring wild subspecies. The wolf is the largest wild extant member of the family Canidae, and is further distinguished from other Canis species by its less pointed ears and muzzle, as well as a shorter torso and a longer tail. The wolf is nonetheless related closely enough to smaller Canis species, such as the coyote and the golden jackal, to produce fertile hybrids with them. The wolf's fur is usually mottled white, brown, grey, and black, although subspecies in the arctic region may be nearly all white.
